clinical: Right-sided colon cancer
Cancers of the caecum and ascending colon often cause iron-deficiency anaemia from slow, hidden bleeding, because the lumen is wide and the stool is still liquid, so obstruction is less common.
Caecal volvulus
The caecum is mobile and can twist on itself (caecal volvulus), which blocks the large bowel and can compromise its blood supply.
Crohn disease
Crohn disease most often involves the terminal ileum and caecum, causing right lower abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss.
Loss of the terminal ileum
The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and recycles bile salts, so extensive resection causes B12 deficiency and bile-salt diarrhoea.
Appendicitis pain
Appendicitis usually starts as pain around the umbilicus that moves to the right iliac fossa, where tenderness is greatest at McBurney point.
Appendix obstruction
The narrow lumen can be blocked by a faecal stone (appendicolith) or by swelling of lymphoid follicles, which leads to inflammation and infection.
Digital rectal examination
Tumours in the lower rectum can be felt with a gloved finger on digital rectal examination.
Rectal perforation
A perforation above the peritoneal reflection spills contents into the peritoneal cavity and causes peritonitis; a perforation below it is extraperitoneal.
Anal fissure
An anal fissure is a tear in the lining below the pectinate line, usually in the back midline, causing pain and bleeding on defaecation.
Anal gland abscesses
Infection of the anal glands, which open into the anal sinuses, can form perianal, intersphincteric or ischioanal abscesses.
Rectal varices

In portal hypertension, veins of the rectal venous plexus can dilate into rectal varices. The superior rectal vein drains to the portal system, while the middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the systemic circulation, so this plexus acts as a portosystemic link.
Lymph drainage of the rectum

Lymph from the upper rectum drains up the superior rectal vessels to the mesorectal and inferior mesenteric nodes, whereas lymph from below the pectinate line drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
Internal anal sphincter
The internal anal sphincter provides most of the resting tone of the anal canal, so its damage causes passive leakage of gas and mucus.
Chronic anal fissure
Spasm of the internal anal sphincter is thought to keep chronic anal fissures open, so treatment aims to relax it, for example with topical glyceryl trinitrate or a surgical sphincterotomy.
Obstetric anal sphincter injury
Third- and fourth-degree obstetric perineal tears involve the external anal sphincter, and damage to it can cause faecal incontinence.
Puborectalis and defaecation
Puborectalis pulls the anorectal junction forward to form the anorectal angle, and it relaxes during defaecation to straighten the angle so stool can pass.
Total mesorectal excision
Rectal cancer surgery removes the rectum together with its surrounding fat and fascia, which lowers the risk of local recurrence.
Ischioanal abscess
Infection of the ischioanal fat forms an ischioanal abscess, usually spreading from an infected anal gland, and these abscesses can become large.

parts.description: The ascending colon is the segment of large intestine that runs up the right flank to the right colic (hepatic) flexure, its back surface lying retroperitoneally. Its wall is gathered into pouches called haustra because the three taeniae coli are shorter than the wall, and the creases between them are the semilunar folds. On abdominal X-ray the haustra give a segmented outline, which is lost in chronic ulcerative colitis (the 'lead-pipe' colon). It is supplied by the ileocolic and right colic arteries.

The taenia libera, or free taenia, is the anterior of the three taeniae coli, the bands into which the longitudinal muscle of the colon is gathered. It runs down the front of the ascending colon and along the lower border of the transverse colon, and it is not attached to the mesocolon or the greater omentum, so it appears as a free, unattached band. Surgeons follow it down the caecum to find the base of the appendix, where all three taeniae converge.

The taenia mesocolica is the posterior of the three taeniae coli, the band of longitudinal muscle to which the mesocolon, the peritoneal fold that suspends the colon, is attached. On the transverse colon this line marks the attachment of the transverse mesocolon, while on the ascending colon, which lies behind the peritoneum, the band faces the posterior abdominal wall. Like the other two taeniae, it converges on the base of the appendix and helps pucker the colon into haustra.

The taenia omentalis is the taenia to which the greater omentum, the apron of fat that hangs from the stomach, is attached along the transverse colon. Because the omentum is fixed to this band, its line of attachment is a useful landmark for picking out this taenia on the transverse colon. The same band continues over the caecum and ascending colon, where it converges with the other two taeniae at the base of the appendix.

The ileal mucosa is the inner lining of the ileum, the last part of the small intestine. It is covered by villi that are shorter than those of the jejunum and lined with absorptive enterocytes (cells that absorb nutrients) and many goblet cells, while its plicae circulares (permanent circular folds) are fewer and smaller. Its lamina propria (connective tissue beneath the epithelium) and submucosa contain Peyer patches, oval lymphoid nodules most numerous on the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum.

The upper lip of the ileocaecal valve, also called the ileocolic lip, is the upper margin of the slit-like ileal orifice, the opening where the terminal ileum enters the caecum. Like the lower lip, it is a flap of mucosa, submucosa and circular muscle that projects into the caecum at the ileocolic junction. Together the two lips form a flap-like sphincter that slows ileal emptying and largely stops colonic contents from refluxing back into the ileum.

The lower lip of the ileocaecal valve, also called the ileocaecal lip, forms the lower margin of the slit-like ileal orifice on the medial wall of the caecum. Like the upper lip, it is a fold of mucosa, submucosa and circular muscle, and together the two lips make up the ileocaecal valve. At colonoscopy the valve looks like a small papilla with a slit-like opening, and the endoscopist passes through it to inspect and biopsy the terminal ileum, for example in Crohn's disease.

The frenula of the ileocaecal valve (singular frenulum, Latin for 'little bridle') are two small mucosal folds, one at each end of the ileal orifice where the upper and lower lips join. Each marks one corner of the slit-like opening and so helps define the limits of the valve on the caecal wall. They are minor features, and the valve is recognised mainly by its two lips and slit-shaped orifice.

The appendiceal mucosa is the lining of the vermiform appendix, the narrow blind tube that hangs from the caecum. It is colonic-type mucosa, with straight, tubular crypts lined with many goblet cells that secrete mucus, and it has no villi; its lumen is narrow and often irregular, and it may be partly obliterated in older people. Beneath the epithelium, the lamina propria and submucosa are packed with lymphoid follicles, so the appendix is part of the gut's immune system.

The lymphoid follicles of the appendix are aggregated nodules of lymphocytes, many with pale germinal centres where B lymphocytes multiply, forming an almost continuous ring within the mucosa and submucosa. This makes the appendix a major site of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), and the follicles are most abundant in childhood and adolescence, shrinking with age. Their hyperplasia (enlargement) after a viral infection is a common cause of luminal obstruction and appendicitis in the young.

The inferior transverse rectal fold is the lowest of the three transverse folds of the rectum (Houston's valves), a permanent crescentic shelf of mucosa, submucosa and circular muscle in the lower rectum. Like the other two folds, it helps support the faecal mass and keeps flatus separate from faeces, and the three folds together correspond to the lateral bends of the rectum. At sigmoidoscopy it appears as a crescentic ridge that the instrument must be angled around.

The anal columns (of Morgagni) are six to ten vertical ridges of mucosa in the upper part of the anal canal, separated from one another by the anal sinuses. Each column contains a terminal branch of the superior rectal artery and vein, and the submucosal anal cushions lie beneath them. Their lining changes from rectal columnar epithelium above, through the anal transitional zone, to non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium below.

The anal valves are small crescent-shaped folds of mucosa that join the lower ends of neighbouring anal columns. Their free lower edges form the pectinate (dentate) line, and each valve forms the lower wall of the anal sinus lying above it. This line marks the junction between the upper, columnar-type lining and the lower, squamous lining, so it is the key landmark for distinguishing internal from external haemorrhoids and for locating anal fissures.

The submucosa is the layer of loose connective tissue between the rectal mucosa and the muscularis externa, allowing the mucosa to move and fold over the muscle. It carries the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, a network of nerve cells that regulates local gut secretion and blood flow, together with blood vessels and lymphatics. In the upper anal canal it thickens to form the vascular anal cushions, and in histology it appears as a loose, pink-staining connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa.

The internal rectal venous plexus is the network of submucosal veins of the rectum and anal canal, arranged mainly as three anal cushions. Each cushion is a mass of thin-walled, blood-filled sinusoids beneath the anal columns, lying at the left lateral, right anterior and right posterior positions. The cushions drain to the superior rectal vein (portal system) and link with the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic system), forming a portosystemic connection. Enlargement and downward slipping of these cushions cause internal haemorrhoids (piles).

The external rectal venous plexus is the network of subcutaneous veins around the anal verge, lying below the pectinate line beneath the perianal skin. Its veins drain through the inferior rectal veins to the internal pudendal and internal iliac veins, so their blood returns to the systemic circulation. External haemorrhoids form here, and because they lie under sensitive skin, a thrombosed one appears as a painful, bluish lump that is usually treated early by incision.

The circular muscle of the rectum is the inner layer of the muscularis externa, a sheet of smooth muscle whose fibres encircle the bowel wall. Its contraction narrows the lumen and helps propel faeces towards the anal canal, under involuntary enteric and autonomic control. It forms the core of the transverse rectal folds and is continued downward as the internal anal sphincter.

The deep part of the external anal sphincter is the upper, ring-shaped portion of the voluntary sphincter, lying just outside the internal sphincter around the upper anal canal. Made of skeletal muscle, it is supplied by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2–4), and it is continuous above with puborectalis to form the anorectal ring. Its contraction closes the upper canal under voluntary control.

The subcutaneous part of the external anal sphincter is the lowest, voluntary portion of that muscle, a ring of skeletal muscle just beneath the perianal skin. It lies below the internal anal sphincter, from which it is separated by the intersphincteric (white) line, which can be felt on examination. As skeletal muscle under voluntary control, it contributes to the squeeze that keeps the anal canal closed, and conjoint longitudinal fibres pierce it on their way to the skin.

Levator ani is the main muscular floor of the pelvis, a sheet of skeletal muscle formed by pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus and puborectalis. It slopes down from the tendinous arch over obturator internus to the anorectal junction and anococcygeal ligament, supporting the pelvic organs and separating the mesorectum above from the ischioanal fossa below. It is supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3–4), and weakness after childbirth or with age can cause pelvic organ prolapse.

The superior rectal vein is the main vein draining the rectum and its venous plexus, running up through the mesorectum alongside the superior rectal artery. It drains into the inferior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic vein, and so its blood reaches the hepatic portal vein and passes through the liver. This is why cancers of the upper rectum and colon tend to spread to the liver, whereas low rectal and anal cancers can reach the lungs through the systemic veins.
